guides.title: How Long Do Running Shoes Last? Miles, Signs, and the Foam
guides.excerpt: Most running shoes last 300 to 500 miles. Check them at 300 and replace them when the foam creases deep, the outsole wears through or your legs feel beaten up on easy runs.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Most running shoes last 300 to 500 miles. Check them at 300 and replace them when the midsole creases deep, the outsole wears through to foam or easy runs start to feel harsh.

## 300 to 500 miles is a range, not a deadline

The range is wide because foam, rubber and runners differ. A heavier runner compresses the midsole more each stride. A runner who scuffs a heel on pavement wears the outsole faster than one who lands softly on trails.

Treat 300 miles as the first check and 500 as the point to replace without more debate. Lab tests show midsole foam loses cushioning with use, but no study gives a mileage that fits every runner.

## Four signs that beat the odometer

- The midsole is creased: press a thumb into the foam. Deep wrinkles across it and a dead feel mean the bounce is gone.
- The outsole is worn through to foam at the heel or under the ball of the foot. Grip and protection go with it.
- The upper has failed: a collapsed heel counter or a torn toe box lets your foot slide.
- Your legs feel more beaten up after easy runs, and the shoe is past 300 miles. A hard training week can do the same, so it's a hint, not proof.

A side-by-side test settles it. Run the same easy route in the old pair one day and a newer pair the next. If the old one feels flat, replace it.

Pain that keeps coming back is a question for a doctor or physical therapist, not a shoe swap.

## Soft shoes wear out sooner than firm ones

A firm shoe feels about the same at mile 1 and mile 300. A soft one changes more, because the foam is the ride. The [Nike Winflo 12](/shoes/nike-winflo-12) is firm with a durable outsole and ages well. The [Hoka Clifton 11](/shoes/hoka-clifton-11) is 42 mm of soft EVA, and you'll feel it go flat.

Daily trainers built for mileage, like the [Nike Pegasus 42](/shoes/nike-pegasus-42), list durability as a strength in our data.

## Two pairs last longer than one

Alternating pairs gives the foam a day to recover between runs. A 2015 study of 264 runners over 22 weeks found those who rotated more than one pair had a 39% lower injury risk (Malisoux and colleagues). It was observational, so it can't prove the rotation caused it. [Rotating two pairs](/rundown/shoe-rotation-two-pairs) shows how to set it up.

Write the start date inside the tongue of each pair, log your miles and set an alert at 300. The [Shoe Finder](/tools/shoe-selector) can filter for durable daily trainers when it's time.

guides.title: How Many Gels for a Marathon? The Count by Finish Time
guides.excerpt: Plan on 60 grams of carbs an hour from 30 minutes in. With 25-gram gels that's 7 gels for a 3:30 marathon, 8 for 4:00 and 11 for 5:00.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Plan on 60 grams of carbs an hour from 30 minutes in. With 25-gram gels that's 7 gels for a 3:30 marathon, 8 for 4:00 and 11 for 5:00.

## Count grams first, then divide by your gel

The gels in our [gel table](/fuel) carry 17 to 40 grams of carbs each, so the number of packets depends on which gel you carry. Start from grams per hour and divide.

60 grams an hour is the usual target for races of two to three hours (Jeukendrup, Sports Medicine, 2014). Runners out for four hours or more can build toward 90 grams an hour, but only with gels that mix glucose and fructose, and only after practicing it.

## Gels by finish time

These counts start at 30 minutes, keep 60 grams an hour and stop 20 minutes from the finish.

- 3:00: 6 gels of 25 g, or 6 of 22 g
- 3:30: 7 gels of 25 g, or 8 of 22 g
- 4:00: 8 gels of 25 g, or 9 of 22 g
- 4:30: 9 gels of 25 g, or 11 of 22 g
- 5:00: 11 gels of 25 g, or 12 of 22 g

The [Maurten Gel 100](/fuel/gels/maurten-gel-100) and the Clif Shot are 25 g. The [GU Original](/fuel/gels/gu-original-energy-gel) is 22 g. A 30 g gel such as the [Precision Fuel PF 30](/fuel/gels/precision-fuel-pf-30-gel) brings a 4:00 marathon down to 7 packets.

Sports drink from the course counts too. Look up the drink's carbs per cup on the race website and skip one gel for every 25 grams you expect to drink.

## First gel at 30 minutes, then on a clock

- Take the first gel about 30 minutes in, before you feel hungry.
- Space the rest evenly: every 25 minutes with 25 g gels, every 22 minutes with 22 g gels, every 30 minutes with 30 g gels.
- Take each one at an aid station with a few sips of water.
- Skip the last 20 minutes. A gel that late does little before the finish.
- Set watch alerts or write the times on your arm. Late gels are the most common way a plan falls apart.

For a schedule with times and miles filled in, open the [4:00 marathon fuel plan](/fuel/plan/marathon/4-00) or enter your own goal in the [Fuel Finder](/tools/fueling). Both adjust the target for your experience, so their counts can run a gel or two higher.

## The count only works if you've practiced it

A stomach that has never taken 60 grams an hour at marathon pace often refuses it on race day. Build up over six to eight weeks of long runs, using the exact gel you'll race with. [Training your gut for race fueling](/rundown/train-your-gut-race-fueling) has the week-by-week build.

This plan is wrong for two groups:

- Half marathoners and 10K runners. Two gels at most cover a half, and a 10K needs none.
- Runners with diabetes or another condition that changes how you handle carbs. Set the target with your doctor or a dietitian.

guides.title: How Many Gels for a Half Marathon? Two for Most Runners
guides.excerpt: Two gels cover most half marathons: one at 40 minutes and one at 70. Add a third if you'll be out past 2:15, and under 1:20 you can skip them.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Two gels cover most half marathons: one at 40 minutes and one at 70. Add a third if you'll be out past 2:15, and under 1:20 you can skip them.

## A half needs 30 to 60 grams of carbs an hour

Sports nutrition guidance puts races of one to two and a half hours at 30 to 60 grams of carbs an hour. Under an hour the benefit is small. A half marathon sits in that middle band for almost everyone, so it needs far less than a marathon plan.

Most gels in our [gel table](/fuel) carry 22 to 25 grams. Two 25 g gels in a 1:45 race is 50 grams, about 29 grams an hour. That's the low end of the band, and enough for most runners at that distance.

## Gels by finish time

- Under 1:20: none needed. Your stored carbs cover the race. Take one at 40 minutes if it helps you mentally.
- 1:20 to 1:45: two gels, at about 40 and 70 minutes.
- 1:45 to 2:15: two or three, at 40, 70 and 100 minutes. Take the third if you feel flat at 100.
- Over 2:15: one every 40 to 45 minutes, which is three or four.

Each of these finish times has a full plan with miles and a packing list: [1:45](/fuel/plan/half-marathon/1-45), [2:00](/fuel/plan/half-marathon/2-00) and [2:15](/fuel/plan/half-marathon/2-15).

## Choose the gel by caffeine, sodium and thickness

- Caffeine: the [caffeinated gels](/fuel/best/caffeinated-gels) in our table range from 25 to 100 mg. If you don't drink coffee, take half a dose or skip it.
- Sodium: our gels carry 0 to 245 mg each. A salty gel helps on a hot day and makes little difference on a cool one.
- Thickness: the 40 g Maurten Gel 160 is a lot to swallow at once. Thinner gels go down easier. Take any gel with a few sips of water.

For more carbs per packet, the [30 g gels](/fuel/best/30g-carb-gels) let two packets do the work of three.

## Try both gels on a long run first

Eat your usual breakfast two to three hours before the start. Use only a gel you've taken in training: race day is a bad time to learn that a flavor or brand upsets your stomach.

If gels have given you trouble before, [training your gut for race fueling](/rundown/train-your-gut-race-fueling) shows how to build up. Carry a spare in your pocket either way. If you feel strong at 100 minutes, you won't need it.

guides.title: How to Find Your Running Cadence and Pick Songs to Match
guides.excerpt: Count your right foot for 30 seconds and multiply by four. Then pick songs at that BPM, and if you want to change it, go up 3 to 5% at a time.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Count how many times your right foot lands in 30 seconds and multiply by four. Pick songs at that BPM, and if you want a higher cadence, raise it 3 to 5% at a time.

## Count 30 seconds of steps

- Warm up for ten minutes at your usual easy pace.
- On a flat stretch, count your right foot landing for 30 seconds.
- Multiply by four. That's steps per minute, which is what cadence means.
- Repeat on another day and at a faster pace.

Cadence rises as you speed up. An easy run in the 160s can turn into the 170s or 180s on a tempo run, and good runners fall outside both ranges. If your watch reports cadence, check it against one hand count to be sure it reads steps, not strides.

## Small changes are the only ones worth making

A 2011 lab study (Heiderscheit and colleagues, University of Wisconsin) ran 45 recreational runners at their normal step rate and at 5% and 10% above and below it. A 5% rise cut the load the knee absorbed. A 10% rise cut hip load too.

The authors also noted that a big change from your natural rate is hard to hold. It was one lab study at a fixed speed, so it doesn't set a target. From a natural 158, a goal of 166 is a reasonable experiment, and 180 is a different way of running.

## Songs at your cadence feel like they run with you

A track at 165 BPM fits a runner at 165 steps a minute. That's why a playlist matched to your number works better than a random shuffle. The [Music Finder](/tools/music) builds one from a BPM or a pace, and the [easy run playlist](/music/workout/easy-run) is a ready-made starting point.

Half-time songs double the choice. A track at 85 BPM matches 170 steps if one foot lands on the beat and the other between beats, so slower songs work too. [170 BPM running songs](/rundown/170-bpm-running-songs) explains where that popular number comes from.

## To raise cadence, add songs 3 to 5% faster

- Pick songs 3 to 5% above your count. At 160, that's 165 to 168 BPM, such as the [165 BPM list](/music/bpm/165).
- Run to them for the last few minutes of an easy run, not the whole run.
- Do it once or twice a week. Your step rate drifts up without thinking about it.
- If the beat feels like a leash, go back to your own rhythm.

Your stride gets a little shorter as cadence rises. That's the trade, and it's the reason to keep changes small. Pain is a question for a doctor or physical therapist, not a cadence app.

guides.title: 170 BPM Running Songs and Why 170 Keeps Coming Up
guides.excerpt: 170 steps a minute is a reasonable target for many easy runs, but it comes from a rough compromise, not a rule. Count your own cadence first and pick songs within a few BPM of it.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** 170 BPM suits many runners at an easy to steady pace, but it's a compromise, not a rule. Count your own cadence first and use songs within 3 to 5 BPM of it.

## 170 is a compromise between two findings

The first is Jack Daniels, the running coach and physiologist, who counted the steps of runners at the 1984 Olympics and found nearly all of them near 180 a minute. Those were elite runners at race pace. Slower runners take fewer, shorter steps.

The second is a 2011 lab study (Heiderscheit and colleagues). Raising step rate by 5% cut the load the knee absorbed in 45 recreational runners, and 10% cut hip load as well. It was one short lab session, not a season of running.

Put together, 170 lands between what casual runners do and what elites do. That's the whole story behind the number.

## Count your own cadence before building a playlist

Run a steady, flat stretch at your normal pace. Count your steps for 30 seconds and double it. Many recreational runners at easy pace land in the 160s, and cadence climbs as you speed up.

If you count 164, songs at 170 feel like a push. Pick music near your own number instead. The [9:00 per mile playlist](/music/pace/9-00-min-mile) and the other pace pages group songs by the pace you run, so you don't have to convert. [How to find your running cadence](/rundown/how-to-find-your-running-cadence) covers the count in more detail.

## Three ways to use 170 BPM songs

- Start 3 to 5 BPM above your current cadence. Your steps drift toward the beat without effort.
- Save the faster songs for the last third of a run, when form tends to slip.
- Use half-time tracks. A song at 85 BPM works at 170 steps if you land one step on the beat and one between.

The [170 BPM page](/music/bpm/170) lists songs at that tempo, with neighbors at [168](/music/bpm/168) and [171](/music/bpm/171) for variety. [Pop at 170 to 180 BPM](/music/genre/pop/170-180-bpm) is the deepest genre in this range. The [Music Finder](/tools/music) builds a full playlist at your number.

## When 170 is the wrong target

- Run-walk beginners. Match the cadence you have, which may be well under 170.
- Long easy runs where you're keeping heart rate low. A list near 160 keeps you from speeding up.
- Fast racing. At 7:00 per mile or quicker most runners are already above 170.

Cadence changes don't treat pain. If something hurts, stop and see a doctor or physical therapist.

For a first try, pick a dozen songs within a few BPM of your count and run an easy 30 minutes to them. If the beat feels hurried, drop 5 BPM and try again.

guides.title: Stability Shoes vs Neutral: Who Needs Support
guides.excerpt: Most runners don't need a stability shoe. A 2014 study of 927 beginners found pronated feet were not injured more often in a neutral shoe, so pick by comfort and keep support for runners with a reason.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Start in a neutral daily trainer and switch to a stability shoe only with a reason, such as feeling unsteady late in long runs. Arch shape and pronation don't predict who needs support.

## Pronation didn't predict injuries in the biggest study

In 2014 a Danish team led by Rasmus Nielsen followed 927 beginners for a year, all in the same neutral shoe (British Journal of Sports Medicine). Runners with pronated feet were not injured more often than runners with neutral feet.

It's one study of beginners in one shoe. Researchers such as Benno Nigg argue that comfort is a better guide than any foot measurement, though that case rests on smaller studies. The practical result: the shoe you stop noticing is usually the right one.

## Stability shoes now weigh and cost the same as neutral ones

A stability shoe adds a firmer or wider inner side to limit how far your foot rolls inward. Current models do it gently, and they cost and weigh about the same as the neutral [Brooks Ghost 18](/shoes/brooks-ghost-18) at $150 and 9.8 oz:

- [Brooks Adrenaline GTS 26](/shoes/brooks-adrenaline-gts-26): $155, 10.8 oz, 10 mm drop
- [ASICS GT-2000 15](/shoes/asics-gt-2000-15): $140, 9.6 oz, 39 mm stack
- [Hoka Arahi 9](/shoes/hoka-arahi-9): $150, 9.7 oz, roomy forefoot
- [Saucony Guide 19](/shoes/saucony-guide-19): $145, 9.4 oz, a stable, planted ride

The heavy end is the [Brooks Beast GTS 24](/shoes/brooks-beast-gts-24): $160, 12.0 oz and motion control. Our data calls it overbuilt for mild pronation, so most runners shouldn't start there.

## Runners with a reason for support

- Your feet or lower legs feel unsteady late in long runs in neutral shoes, and a supportive pair fixes it.
- A coach, physical therapist or shop that watched you run gives a specific reason.
- You're a heavier runner who likes a wide, planted platform. The [stability shoes for heavy runners](/shoes/best/stability-running-shoes-for-heavy-runners) list is a starting point.
- You prefer the feel. That's a valid reason, and the comfort research backs it.

## Pick by a comfort test, not an arch test

Try one neutral shoe and one or two stability shoes with similar cushion. Jog a few minutes in each, in the store or at home within the return window. Take the one you notice least. If they feel the same, take the neutral one.

A stability shoe won't fix pain. If something hurts, see a doctor or physical therapist. If you switch from neutral, run one or two easy runs in the new pair before a long run. The [Shoe Finder](/tools/shoe-selector) lets you set stability as a preference and compare specs.

guides.title: Best Running Shoes for Beginners: Pick for Fit, Then Price
guides.excerpt: Your first pair should be a neutral daily trainer that fits the day you try it on. The Brooks Ghost 18 at $150 is our default, and the Nike Winflo 12 at $110 is the cheaper way in.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Buy a neutral daily trainer that fits the day you try it on. The Brooks Ghost 18 ($150) is our default, the Nike Winflo 12 ($110) the cheaper pick and the Hoka Clifton 11 ($150) the softer one.

## Fit decides it, because the specs barely differ

Beginner trainers sit in a narrow band. The Brooks Ghost 18 has a 36 mm stack and a 12 mm drop, and the [Nike Pegasus 42](/shoes/nike-pegasus-42) has 37 mm and 10 mm. A new runner won't feel that gap, but a pinched toe shows up in the first mile.

Check these in the store or in the first ten minutes at home:

- A thumb's width of room past your longest toe
- No heel slip when you walk fast or jog
- Nothing rubs or presses anywhere
- Tried on in the afternoon, when feet are bigger, with the socks you'll run in

A shoe that feels almost right on day one feels wrong by mile four. Keep the box and the receipt until you've run in it.

## Three first shoes worth buying

- [Brooks Ghost 18](/shoes/brooks-ghost-18), $150, 9.8 oz. Neutral, moderate cushion, a durable outsole and wide sizes. It plays it safe: firmer and less bouncy than max-cushion shoes.
- [Nike Winflo 12](/shoes/nike-winflo-12), $110, 9.7 oz. Firmer foam and a durable outsole. Not built for workouts, which doesn't matter for three easy runs a week.
- [Hoka Clifton 11](/shoes/hoka-clifton-11), $150, 9.7 oz, 42 mm stack. The soft one, comfortable for walking and standing too. It feels sluggish at faster paces.

Try on the Ghost and the Clifton side by side and buy the one your feet stop noticing. If $150 is too much, the Winflo is the pick, and [our under-$120 guide](/rundown/good-running-shoes-under-120) has four more.

## What a first pair can skip

- Carbon-plated racers. They're built for race day and cost $250 and up. [Choosing your first racing shoe](/rundown/how-to-choose-your-first-racing-shoe) covers when one makes sense.
- Stability shoes, unless a neutral shoe has given you a reason. [Stability vs neutral](/rundown/stability-shoes-vs-neutral-do-you-need-support) explains who needs support.
- The lightest shoe on the wall. At 9.7 to 9.8 oz, all three picks are light enough for easy running.

## Your second pair will be a better buy

After a month of running you'll know whether you like soft or firm, roomy or snug. That makes the second purchase easier than the first. The [Shoe Finder](/tools/shoe-selector) narrows the list by your foot, your runs and your budget in a couple of minutes.

guides.title: Heel Drop Explained: Does 4mm vs 10mm Matter for You?
guides.excerpt: Heel drop shifts work between your calves and your knees, and the injury research is thin. Stay within 4 mm of the drop you run in now, and change it slowly if you change it at all.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Heel drop shifts load between your calves and your knees, and no trial shows one drop is safer. Buy within 4 mm of the drop you run in pain-free now, and change it over weeks if you change it.

## Drop is heel height minus forefoot height

A 12 mm drop means your heel sits 12 mm higher than the ball of your foot. Zero drop means they sit level. Shoes at the same price cover the whole range:

- [Brooks Ghost 18](/shoes/brooks-ghost-18): 12 mm, $150
- [Nike Pegasus 42](/shoes/nike-pegasus-42): 10 mm, $145
- [Saucony Guide 19](/shoes/saucony-guide-19): 6 mm, $145
- Saucony Kinvara 16: 4 mm, $130
- [Altra Torin 9](/shoes/altra-torin-9): 0 mm, $150

Brands have house habits. In our data, Nike's running shoes run 6 to 10 mm, Hoka's 5 to 8 and Altra's 0 to 4. Brooks ranges from 6 to 12. If you've only bought one brand, you may have run in a narrow slice of this range without knowing it.

## What drop changes

A higher heel moves load toward the knee and away from the calf and Achilles tendon. A lower drop does the reverse. That's why runners who jump from 12 mm to 0 mm often get tight calves for a few weeks.

Drop doesn't decide how you land. Speed, cadence and habit set that, and plenty of heel strikers run in 4 mm shoes.

The injury evidence is thin. The studies are small and measure joint loads in a lab, not injuries over a season. If pain lingers, see a doctor or physical therapist rather than shopping for a new drop.

## Stack height changes the feel too

Two shoes with the same drop can feel nothing alike. The [New Balance More v6](/shoes/new-balance-fresh-foam-x-more-v6) has a 4 mm drop on a 43 mm stack. The [Altra Escalante 5](/shoes/altra-escalante-5) is zero drop on 24 mm. Compare both numbers.

## Stay within 4 mm of what works

Find the drop of the shoe you've run in pain-free for six months and shop within 4 mm of it. A Ghost runner can move to a Pegasus without thinking. A runner on 10 mm shoes going straight to a zero-drop Torin is the switch that causes trouble.

The exception: if your knees complain on downhills in a 12 mm shoe but your calves never do, a lower drop is a fair experiment.

## Switch drop over weeks, not runs

- Keep the old pair and add the new one. A [two-pair rotation](/rundown/shoe-rotation-two-pairs) makes this easy.
- Start with one short easy run a week in the lower drop.
- Add a second run after two weeks without soreness. Do long runs in it last.
- Sore calves the next day mean slow down. Sharp pain, or soreness that lasts several days, means see a professional.

Going from 10 mm to 4 mm usually takes a month on this plan. Going to zero, give it two. The [Shoe Finder](/tools/shoe-selector) filters by drop alongside cushion and fit.

guides.title: Good Running Shoes Under $120: What You Give Up, What You Don't
guides.excerpt: The Nike Winflo 12 at $110 is the default under $120. Cheaper shoes give up the newest bouncy foams, not fit, durability or light weight.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** The Nike Winflo 12 ($110) is the default under $120. Cheaper shoes give up the newest bouncy foams, not fit, durability or weight.

## Under $120 you lose bounce and little else

The ten most popular daily trainers in our data average $151.50. One shelf down, most of the difference is foam. Budget midsoles are firmer EVA blends: durable and predictable, without the spring of a $170 trainer. You notice it most late in long runs.

Weight is close. The $110 [Winflo 12](/shoes/nike-winflo-12) is 9.7 oz, and the $145 Pegasus 42 is 9.8 oz. Fit and durability don't drop with price either, and no study has shown that pricier shoes lower injury risk.

## Five worth buying

- Nike Winflo 12, $110, 9.7 oz, 10 mm drop. Moderate cushion and a durable outsole. The pick if you're not sure what you want.
- [ASICS GT-1000 15](/shoes/asics-gt-1000-15), $100, 9.4 oz. Moderate support for $100, tied with its older version as the cheapest in our data. The pick if you want a stability shoe.
- [Brooks Launch 12](/shoes/brooks-launch-12), $115, 8.5 oz. Firm and quick, light enough for strides and tempo runs. Firm for long runs.
- [Brooks Revel 9](/shoes/brooks-revel-9), $100, 8.7 oz. A flexible, light shoe that doubles as an everyday sneaker. Firm over long distances.
- [New Balance Fresh Foam 680 v9](/shoes/new-balance-fresh-foam-680-v9), $85, 9.1 oz. Soft, comes in several widths, and the best value in the group.

The Nike Revolution 8 at $70 sits one step below: firm, basic cushioning and not built for long runs. Prices are list prices from our data, and all five are often on sale for less. The full list is on [running shoes under $120](/shoes/best/running-shoes-under-120).

## When paying more makes sense

- You run more than about 35 miles a week. Softer foam helps on tired legs.
- You've found a fit nothing cheaper matches.
- You're adding a second, faster shoe. A [two-pair rotation](/rundown/shoe-rotation-two-pairs) built on a $110 trainer and a $150 one beats one $260 shoe doing every job.

The [Shoe Finder](/tools/shoe-selector) matches shoes to your feet and your week, and takes a budget if you give it one.

guides.title: How to Train Your Gut for Race Fueling in Six to Eight Weeks
guides.excerpt: Your gut adapts to carbs taken while running. Fuel every long run for six to eight weeks, building from 30 to 60 grams an hour with the gels you'll race with.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Your gut adapts to carbs taken while running. Fuel every long run for six to eight weeks, building from 30 to 60 grams an hour with the exact gels you'll race with.

## Practice raises how much your gut can take

Regular carbs during exercise increase how much sugar the gut absorbs. Four weeks of high-carb training raised carb use during exercise in trained cyclists (Cox and colleagues, 2010). Two weeks of repeated carbs during running cut gut symptoms in a small group of runners (Costa and colleagues, 2017).

The adaptation is specific to effort. Hard running pulls blood away from the gut, so a gel on an easy jog says little about a gel at marathon pace. Practice some of it at race effort.

## The six to eight week build

- Weeks 1 and 2: fuel on every run over 75 minutes at 30 to 40 grams an hour. One 25 g gel every 40 minutes does it.
- Weeks 3 and 4: raise it to 50 to 60 grams an hour. Take at least one gel during the hard part of a workout.
- Week 5 on: hold 60 grams an hour on every long run.
- Going past 60 toward 90 grams: only for races over about 3:30, and only with gels that mix glucose and fructose. The label lists maltodextrin or glucose plus fructose.

Our [Fuel Finder](/tools/fueling) turns a distance and finish time into a schedule you can follow on these runs.

## Rehearse the race, not just the gel

- Use the exact product, flavor and caffeine dose you'll race with.
- Carry the gels where you'll carry them on race day.
- Open one at pace, with cold fingers if the race will be cold.
- Wash each gel down with water. Gel plus sports drink stacks sugar on sugar.

By the taper, 60 grams an hour should feel routine.

## Fixes when a session goes wrong

- Sloshing stomach: too much at once. Take smaller amounts more often.
- Cramping or a rush to the toilet: often a high-caffeine gel or a fructose-heavy one before your gut adapted. Switch to [caffeine-free gels](/fuel/best/caffeine-free-gels) for two weeks, then build again.
- Nausea at hard effort: usually fuel taken too late. Start earlier and go smaller.
- Symptoms that keep coming back after weeks of practice: see a doctor or a sports dietitian.

## Pair it with a race plan

Gut training sets your ceiling. The race plan uses it. [How many gels for a marathon](/rundown/how-many-gels-for-a-marathon) gives the count by finish time, and [race-day fueling mistakes](/rundown/race-day-fueling-mistakes) lists the five habits that undo the practice.

guides.title: Running Shoe Rotation: Two Pairs Cover Almost Everyone
guides.excerpt: A daily trainer for most miles plus a lighter shoe for fast days is a full rotation. Add a third pair only for racing, trails or an early replacement.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Two pairs make a rotation: a daily trainer for about 80% of your miles and a lighter shoe for fast days. Add a third only for racing, trails or overlapping a worn-out pair.

## Rotating spreads the load and rests the foam

Different shoes load your legs differently. A 4 mm drop puts more work on the calf than a 10 mm drop, and a firm shoe asks more of your feet than a soft one. Alternating spreads the stress instead of repeating one pattern every day.

The evidence is one study: 264 runners over 22 weeks, where those who rotated more than one pair had a 39% lower injury risk (Malisoux and colleagues, 2015). It was observational, so treat it as a hint. Foam also rebounds between runs, so each pair runs closer to how it was built.

## Pair one is a daily trainer

Durable, comfortable at easy pace and stable when you're tired. Popular choices from our data:

- [Brooks Ghost 18](/shoes/brooks-ghost-18): $150, 9.8 oz
- [Nike Pegasus 42](/shoes/nike-pegasus-42): $145, 9.8 oz
- [Hoka Clifton 11](/shoes/hoka-clifton-11): $150, 9.7 oz, the softest of the three

## Pair two is lighter, for fast days

It doesn't need a carbon plate. A light trainer with livelier foam changes how intervals and tempo runs feel:

- [Hoka Mach 7](/shoes/hoka-mach-7): $145, 8.3 oz, handles easy pace through tempo
- [Adidas Adizero Evo SL](/shoes/adidas-adizero-evo-sl): $150, 7.9 oz, light for its 39 mm stack

Wear the daily trainer most days and the fast shoe on workout days. With two quality sessions a week, neither midsole runs two days in a row.

## A third pair earns its place in three cases

- You have a goal race within three months and want a plated racer. The [Nike Vaporfly 4](/shoes/nike-vaporfly-4) is $260 and a poor daily trainer, so buy it for races, practice in it twice and save it.
- Your daily trainer is past 300 miles and you've started its replacement. Overlapping old and new is the most useful rotation there is.
- You run trails. Road shoes on wet roots and rock give little grip.

A dedicated recovery shoe isn't on the list. If your daily trainer isn't comfortable on easy days, it's the wrong daily trainer.

## One pair is fine if you run three or four easy days

The second shoe only helps if it gets used. Four easy runs a week works on one good pair plus an early replacement. Foam ages with time as well as miles, so a pair sitting in the closet still wears out. The [Shoe Finder](/tools/shoe-selector) picks a daily trainer and a fast shoe from your answers.

guides.title: A Substitute Teacher and a 45-Year-Old Mom Won the 2026 LA Marathon
guides.excerpt: Nathan Martin, a substitute teacher and high school coach from Michigan, won by 0.01 seconds. Priscah Cherono, 45, led the women's race from mile 1 and beat every man to the tape.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Nathan Martin, a substitute teacher and high school coach from Jackson, Michigan, won the 2026 Los Angeles Marathon by 0.01 seconds. Priscah Cherono, a 45-year-old mother of three, won the women's race and the Marathon Chase bonus.

## The men's race was decided by a hundredth of a second

- Winner: Nathan Martin, USA, 2:11:16.50
- Second: Michael Kamau, Kenya, the same official time to the second
- Margin: 0.01 seconds, the closest finish in the race's history

Kamau led late in the race. Martin closed on him over the final stretch and passed him in the last strides before the line in Century City. Kamau collapsed just after the finish and was taken off on a stretcher. Reports said he had not taken fluids during the race.

Some outlets list Martin's time as 2:11:17 or 2:11:18. The race's own awards page gives 2:11:16.50.

## Martin coaches teenagers between races

Martin works as a substitute teacher and coaches cross-country at Jackson High School. He ran for Spring Arbor University and qualified for the U.S. Olympic Trials in 2016 and 2020. Coverage of the race called him the fastest U.S.-born Black marathoner.

He is the second American man in a row to win in Los Angeles, after Matthew Richtman in 2025.

## Cherono led from mile 1 and beat the men to the tape

- Winner: Priscah Cherono, Kenya, 2:25:20 official
- Second: Kellyn Taylor, USA, 2:27:37
- Gap: 2 minutes 17 seconds

Cherono, 45, lives in Colorado Springs and placed 10th in the 5,000 meters at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. She led from mile 1 to the finish.

Los Angeles runs a "Marathon Chase": the elite women start ahead of the elite men, and the first runner across the line wins a $10,000 bonus. Cherono crossed before any man.

## What it means for the rest of the field

More than 27,000 runners ran from Dodger Stadium to Century City. Kamau's collapse after a race without fluids is the reminder for everyone else: drink and fuel on a schedule, even when you feel fine.

For your own marathon, [how many gels for a marathon](/rundown/how-many-gels-for-a-marathon) gives the count by finish time. [Race-day fueling mistakes](/rundown/race-day-fueling-mistakes) covers the errors that end races early, and the [Fuel Finder](/tools/fueling) builds a schedule for your goal.

guides.title: How to Choose Your First Racing Shoe
guides.excerpt: Buy a racing shoe once you're training for a time, not just a finish. Start with the $175 Saucony Endorphin Speed 6, and move to a $250 carbon super shoe when you know what you like.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Buy a racing shoe once you're training for a time, not just a finish. The Saucony Endorphin Speed 6 ($175) is the forgiving first pick; carbon super shoes start at $250.

## You need one only when the time matters

If you're running your first half or marathon to finish, your daily trainer is the right shoe. Racing shoes give up stability and comfort for speed, and tired, untrained legs feel that trade.

If you're chasing a time, a plated shoe can help. In a 2018 lab study, a Nike prototype improved running economy by 4% on average over two other marathon shoes (Hoogkamer and colleagues). The test ran 18 trained runners at 14 to 18 km/h, about 6:54 to 5:22 per mile, so the effect at slower paces is less certain.

## What makes a racing shoe different

- A stiff plate in the midsole: carbon, or nylon in gentler shoes
- Light foam that returns more energy than a trainer's EVA
- A rocker shape that rolls you forward through each stride
- Less stability and a thinner outsole than a daily trainer

That last point matters for buying. Racing shoes wear faster and cost more, so most runners keep them for races and a few key workouts.

## Four racing shoes from our data

- [Saucony Endorphin Speed 6](/shoes/saucony-endorphin-speed-6), $175, 8.2 oz. A nylon plate makes it more forgiving than carbon, and it's durable enough for regular training. Our pick for a first fast shoe. It fits slightly short, so consider a half size up.
- [Nike Vaporfly 4](/shoes/nike-vaporfly-4), $260, 6.0 oz. The lightest of the four and good across race distances. Narrow fit and a short-lived outsole.
- [Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5](/shoes/adidas-adizero-adios-pro-5), $250, 7.6 oz. Carbon rods instead of a plate and an aggressive forward roll. Best for midfoot and forefoot strikers.
- [Hoka Rocket X 3](/shoes/hoka-rocket-x-3), $250, 7.4 oz. A winged carbon plate makes it unusually stable for a super shoe. The pick if other racers feel wobbly.

More options sit on the [race-day shoes](/shoes/best/race-day-shoes) list, with a narrower set on [race-day shoes under $150](/shoes/best/race-day-shoes-under-150).

## Match it to the race and your legs

For a 5K or 10K, lighter and firmer works. For a marathon, take more cushion: your legs need help at mile 22, not mile 2.

Run at least two or three tempo runs or long runs in the shoe before race day. Calves and feet need time to adjust to a plate and a rocker. Never debut a racing shoe on race day.

guides.title: Race-Day Fueling Mistakes That Wreck a Marathon, and the Fix for Each
guides.excerpt: Most race-day fueling problems come from a new gel, a late first gel, gels without water, no salt in the heat or a fast first half. Each fix can be rehearsed on a long run.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Most marathon fueling problems come from five habits: a new gel on race day, a late first gel, gels without water, no extra sodium in the heat and a first half run too fast. Each fix can be rehearsed on a long run.

## Use only fuel you've trained with

The gel handed out at mile 8 may be a brand your stomach has never met. Check the race website for the course gel and drink, then either train with them or carry your own.

Run your exact race plan on at least three long runs: same gel, same flavor, same timing.

## Take the first gel 30 to 45 minutes in

Hunger shows up after the deficit has started. By then the gel is playing catch-up. Start early and keep a steady clock: 60 grams of carbs an hour is the usual marathon target, which is a 25 g gel every 25 minutes. [How many gels for a marathon](/rundown/how-many-gels-for-a-marathon) has the count for each finish time.

## Wash every gel down with water

A gel is concentrated sugar. Without water it sits in the stomach and can cause nausea or cramping. Take a few sips from a water cup with each one.

Taking a gel with sports drink instead stacks sugar on sugar, which upsets some stomachs. If you want both, take them at different aid stations.

## Add sodium when the day is hot

Sweat salt varies a lot from runner to runner. Our [Fuel Finder](/tools/fueling) suggests 300 to 500 mg of sodium an hour in cool weather and 500 to 700 mg in heat. Gels in our table carry 0 to 245 mg each, so on a hot day a [high-sodium gel](/fuel/best/high-sodium-gels) or an electrolyte drink fills the gap.

The evidence that salt prevents cramps is weak. Late-race cramps track more with fatigue and pace than with sodium, so don't expect salt tabs to fix a race run too fast.

## Run the first half at goal pace or slower

Running faster burns carbohydrate faster. A first half a few minutes ahead of plan spends stores that no gel replaces in time. Even pacing is the safer plan for almost everyone. The [pace calculator](/tools/pace-calculator) gives you per-mile splits to hold.

## Check five things on race morning

- The gel and flavor you used on three or more long runs
- Gel times set as watch alerts or written on your arm
- One spare gel beyond the plan
- Breakfast two to three hours before the start, the same one you eat before long runs
- Course drink and water stations marked on the course map

If your stomach has failed you before, start with [training your gut for race fueling](/rundown/train-your-gut-race-fueling) six to eight weeks out.

guides.title: Spring 2026 Running Shoe Releases: What Came Out and What It Costs
guides.excerpt: The shoes that shipped from February to May 2026, with price and weight from our data, plus when the shoes tipped for spring arrived.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
**Short answer:** Spring 2026's biggest releases were the Hoka Mach 7, ASICS Superblast 3, Brooks Ghost 18 and Nike Pegasus 42. Most racing shoes tipped for spring arrived later, between June and October.

## Daily trainers that shipped in spring

Release dates, prices and weights below are from our shoe data.

- [Hoka Mach 7](/shoes/hoka-mach-7), March: $145, 8.3 oz, 5 mm drop. Light enough for tempo runs, $5 more than the Mach 6.
- [Saucony Guide 19](/shoes/saucony-guide-19), March: $145, 9.4 oz. Moderate support with a planted ride.
- [ASICS Superblast 3](/shoes/asics-superblast-3), April: $200, 8.8 oz on a 45 mm stack. Race-style foam for training miles, at a race-style price.
- ASICS Gel-Cumulus 28, May: $145, 9.2 oz. Middle-of-the-road cushioning that's light for its stack.
- [Brooks Ghost 18](/shoes/brooks-ghost-18) and [Nike Pegasus 42](/shoes/nike-pegasus-42), May: $150 and $145, both 9.8 oz. Small updates to the two most popular daily trainers.

## Racing shoes from early 2026

- Saucony Endorphin Pro 5, February: $230, 7.3 oz, narrow fit
- Puma Deviate Nitro Elite 4, February: $230, 6.9 oz
- Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3, April: $500, 3.4 oz, the lightest shoe in our data

## The shoes tipped for spring came later

In March this guide listed seven shoes expected between March and May. Here is when the four we track arrived:

- Saucony Endorphin Elite 3: June, $275, 7.0 oz
- Brooks Ghost Max 4: August, $160, 10.3 oz
- Brooks Hyperion Elite 6: August, $250, 7.0 oz
- [Saucony Endorphin Speed 6](/shoes/saucony-endorphin-speed-6): October 15, $175, 8.2 oz

The Skechers Aero Burst 2, Brooks Cascadia Elite and Brooks Ghost Trail 2 aren't in our data. The two Brooks models are trail shoes, and we track road shoes.

## Last year's version is often the better buy

Most of these updates are small, and our data says so for several (the Pegasus 42 is an "incremental update over the 41"). When a new version lands, the old one usually drops in price, and the Mach 6, Superblast 2 and Ghost 17 are all still in our data for comparison. The [newest running shoes](/shoes/best/new-running-shoes) list shows every recent release, and the [Shoe Finder](/tools/shoe-selector) compares old and new side by side.
